name: A sugarcane and paddy farmer in Mandya (Old Mysuru region)
definition: Puttaswamy is a composite portrait of a smallholder cultivator in Mandya district's Cauvery-irrigated core, drawn from documented patterns of land, caste and agrarian distress in the Old Mysuru region rather than from any single real person. He is 44 years old and farms roughly 2.5 acres of KRS-canal-fed land in Malavalli taluk, growing sugarcane and paddy in rotation, supplemented by two milch cows sold through a Nandini-affiliated dairy cooperative. He belongs to the Vokkaliga community, which Census-based and political-analysis sources describe as numerically dominant across Mandya, Ramanagara, Mysuru and rural Bengaluru. He lives with his wife Rathnamma, his elderly parents, a sixteen-year-old daughter in the tenth standard, and a thirteen-year-old son in the eighth standard, in a joint household whose annual cash income, after diesel, fertiliser and labour costs, rarely exceeds roughly one and a half lakh rupees, most of it earned once or twice a year at cane harvest and paddy sale. This profile is an analytic composite built from Census, UDISE+ and district-reporting evidence about Mandya, not a record of an identifiable individual.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile:
Puttaswamy's work is organised around two intersecting calendars: the release schedule of Krishna Raja Sagara (KRS) canal water that irrigates his fields, and the 12-to-18-month growth cycle of sugarcane. He rises before 5 a.m. to walk his two cows to graze and to check the inlet channel watering his paddy nursery, then spends the morning in the field with his wife Rathnamma, who does most of the transplanting and weeding while he manages irrigation turns and pesticide application. Mandya district, still widely described as Karnataka's sugar bowl, is the district where sugar factories traditionally announce cane prices first, with other mills across the state following suit. But the announced price is only the start of a long negotiation, because mills routinely delay payment for cane already crushed, leaving farmers carrying arrears through the following season; district administrations have periodically had to order sugar factories to release pending price and subsidy amounts owed to farmers for a completed crushing season, with the state and mills each contributing a share per tonne meant to top up the cane price. Puttaswamy has waited out such delays more than once, borrowing first from a cooperative credit society and, when that ceiling is reached, from a private moneylender at higher interest to cover fertiliser and school costs while the mill payment is pending.

During the harvesting season, which runs roughly from December to March, Puttaswamy also works as an informal contractor for cane-cutting labour, arranging migrant gangs for his own and neighbouring farms. In the lean months between paddy transplantation and cane harvest, he and Rathnamma rely on the fortnightly milk cheque from the dairy cooperative, the household's only predictable income; in at least two bad seasons he has also taken up MGNREGA work on village road and canal-desilting projects to bridge a cash shortfall. Diesel-pump irrigation, since electricity to agricultural feeders is intermittent, is a recurring cost he cannot avoid even when the KRS reservoir is full, and a poor monsoon or an unfavourable Cauvery Water Management Authority release order to Tamil Nadu can cut his second paddy crop altogether, a risk that shapes nearly every financial decision he makes in a given year.

On roughly a third of an acre too far from the canal head to get a reliable water turn, he grows ragi and fodder grass instead of paddy, a hedge against a season when canal releases run short. In a good year, after clearing input costs and cooperative loan instalments, the household is left with perhaps one and a half lakh rupees in cash plus grain and jaggery for home use; in a year of delayed cane payment or a weak monsoon that margin disappears, and the family draws down savings meant for his daughter's college fees or his son's school supplies. He does not consider his household as poor as the tribal households in Chamarajanagara he reads about, but describes the work as one bad season away from serious debt, a description he has heard echoed by fellow farmers at the cane-price protests he periodically joins outside the mill gates.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile:
Puttaswamy's household is a three-generation joint family: he and Rathnamma, his parents (his father can no longer work the fields but still supervises irrigation timing from the field bund), and their two children. Vokkaliga households in the Cauvery basin are documented as predominantly agrarian and rural, with land passed down through sons, and Puttaswamy's own 2.5 acres are already half of what his father once farmed before it was divided between him and his elder brother, who lives in the adjoining house and shares the diesel pump. Rathnamma's day begins earlier than his: she milks the cows, cooks for six people, transplants and weeds alongside him for several hours, and manages the kitchen garden and poultry that supplement the family's diet, a pattern of combined agricultural and domestic labour that district-level demographic accounts of rural Mandya describe as typical for women married into cultivating families, without implying it is universal or equally chosen by all households.

Decisions about the children's education and the daughter's eventual marriage are discussed jointly by Puttaswamy, his father and his brother, reflecting the extended family's continued authority over major household choices even though Rathnamma manages day-to-day domestic and dairy income. The family has not yet fixed a marriage for their daughter Chaitra, but relatives have begun making informal enquiries, a pattern district-level accounts of the Cauvery belt describe as more common once a girl completes secondary school than while she remains enrolled, without dating it to any fixed age. Their son Kiran, as the presumptive inheritor of the family's land once it is his turn to divide it with any future siblings, is already expected to learn cane and paddy cultivation directly from his father and grandfather during school holidays and the harvest season, an apprenticeship that competes directly with his schoolwork.

Caregiving for Puttaswamy's ageing parents falls almost entirely on Rathnamma, since public elder-care or nursing support does not reach a village of this size, and the family has never seriously discussed a nuclear household arrangement, both for cultural reasons and because splitting the small holding further would leave neither son with a genuinely viable farm. Property, including the house itself, remains registered jointly in the name of Puttaswamy's father, a common arrangement in the district that keeps ultimate authority over major decisions, including any future land sale, with the senior generation rather than with Puttaswamy or Rathnamma directly. Rathnamma also manages the household's small cash reserve from milk sales and vegetable-garden produce, a fund she controls more directly than farm income, which passes first through Puttaswamy and his father, and which she draws on for the children's everyday school expenses, illustrating a division of financial authority common in Cauvery-belt farming households where women often manage smaller, steadier income streams while men control the larger, seasonal cash from the main crop.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile:
Puttaswamy studied only up to the seventh standard in the village government school before his father needed him full-time in the fields, a trajectory he does not regret but does not want repeated for his own children. Chaitra, his daughter, completed government Kannada-medium schooling through the tenth standard in the village and has just cleared her SSLC exams; whether she continues to a pre-university college in Malavalli town, about ten kilometres away, depends heavily on transport and safety, since the family will not send her by shared auto or cycle on the highway. The free bus travel Karnataka's Shakti scheme has extended to all women and girls since June 2023 has changed this calculation directly: in its first year the scheme recorded over 225 crore free rides by women statewide, saving beneficiaries a combined 5,481 crore rupees in fares, at an average daily ridership of 18.1 lakh women between June 2023 and March 2024. Puttaswamy now treats a free, subsidised KSRTC bus service to the taluk town as the deciding factor in letting Chaitra pursue PU college rather than stopping her education at SSLC.

His son Kiran's risk of leaving school runs in a different direction. During the cane-harvesting season from December to March, when labour is short and cane-cutting wages rise, neighbouring families with landless or very small holdings routinely pull sons of Kiran's age out of school for weeks at a stretch to work in cutting gangs, or take them along when the family migrates for hired cane-cutting labour elsewhere in Mandya's Malavalli and Maddur taluks, a pattern documented as a recurring cause of secondary-school absenteeism in this part of the district. Puttaswamy's own landholding is just large enough that he has so far kept Kiran in school through the harvest by hiring outside labour instead, but he is aware that a bad cane-payment year could force him to use his son's labour instead of paying wages he cannot yet collect from the mill.

Karnataka's secondary-level dropout rate was recorded at 22.09% for classes 9 and 10 in UDISE+ 2023-24 data, against a 14.1% national average, and more recent UDISE+ figures put the dropout rate among girls in classes 9 and 10 at 13.9%, still above the 8% national average. Mandya district's own numbers are older but illustrative: a district survey conducted in 2013-14 recorded 2,151 out-of-school children aged 6 to 14 in the district, of whom 1,297 were boys and 854 were girls, a reminder that in this Cauvery-belt district boys' dropout linked to farm and cane labour has historically run higher than girls', the reverse of the more recent state-wide gendered pattern. Puttaswamy also worries about the growing gap between the Kannada-medium government schooling his children have received and the English-medium private schooling increasingly demanded by jobs in Bengaluru's economy; relatives working in the city have told him that Kannada-medium graduates from villages like his struggle even for entry-level private-sector jobs. For now, his strategy is to keep both children in school as long as the farm's cash flow allows, treating any dropout as a last resort forced by debt or labour shortage rather than a preference.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile:
For ordinary illness, Puttaswamy's family relies on the primary health centre serving his village cluster, staffed by a doctor who visits on fixed days, and travels to the district hospital in Mandya town or, for anything requiring surgery or specialist care, to Mysuru's referral hospitals when the family can afford the trip and the lost farm labour it costs. The mental strain of debt and price uncertainty is not abstract to him: national human-rights authorities have investigated cane-payment delays in Mandya as a contributing factor in farmer suicides in the district, treating the issue seriously enough to seek explanations from the state government. Partly in response to this kind of agrarian distress, NIMHANS in Bengaluru piloted a telemedicine-based Primary Care Psychiatry Programme with a pilot experience in Mandya district, training local doctors to recognise and treat depression and anxiety in primary care rather than requiring a trip to a psychiatric specialist in the city; the programme later evolved into a year-long diploma course offered more widely. Puttaswamy has never personally visited a counsellor, but a cousin who did described it as the first time anyone in a government clinic had asked him directly about the stress of unpaid cane bills.

Physically, the greatest risks in his working life come from the cane and paddy fields themselves: cuts from sickles during harvest, prolonged exposure to pesticide spray without reliable protective equipment, and the strain of standing in flooded paddy fields for hours, which he and other farmers in the area associate with joint pain in later years, though he has not sought a formal diagnosis for it. Rathnamma's health is the family's lowest priority in practice, even though her working day is longer than his: she attends the primary health centre only when a condition becomes disruptive to her work, a pattern rural health researchers have linked more broadly to the low priority routinely given to women's health within agricultural households in this region. Neither Puttaswamy nor Rathnamma has health insurance beyond the state's public hospital entitlements, and a serious hospitalisation for either of them, or for his elderly parents, is the single financial risk he says worries him more than a bad monsoon.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile:
Puttaswamy identifies as Vokkaliga, a community Census-based and political-analysis sources describe as numerically dominant across Mandya, Ramanagara, Mysuru and rural Bengaluru, historically associated with landholding and cultivation in the Cauvery belt, though such descriptions are demographic generalisations about a large and internally diverse community rather than a claim that every Vokkaliga household farms or holds land. His family's most significant pilgrimage is to the Cheluvanarayana Swamy temple at Melukote for the Vairamudi festival, an occasion regional cultural accounts describe as a major Vokkaliga pilgrimage event in Mandya district, which Puttaswamy's family has attended most years since his childhood. The Adichunchanagiri Mutt, based in Nagamangala, functions in his understanding less as a place of worship than as an institution running schools and hostels drawing Vokkaliga students from villages like his own, and he has considered it as an option for Kiran's secondary schooling if the household's finances tighten further.

Labour on his farm during peak transplantation and harvest periods is not confined to family members: he hires day labourers from Scheduled Caste communities in his village, most often people identifying as Holeya, one of the Scheduled Caste communities the Census records as present across all six Old Mysuru districts, generally in a wage-labour rather than landowning relationship to farmers like himself, a structural pattern regional social-science literature describes without treating it as fixed or unchangeable. Puttaswamy's own social world outside the immediate family runs mainly through the village's farmers' cooperative society, informal caste-based mutual-aid networks that help arrange loans and marriages, and seasonal festivals tied to the sowing and harvest calendar, including local village-deity festivals that double as occasions for settling small community disputes. He is aware, mostly through television and conversations at the mill gate, of the ongoing political demand by Vokkaliga organisations for a larger quota under the state's backward-classes reservation framework, and supports it, though he describes the everyday texture of his community life as shaped far more by land, water and the cooperative society than by reservation politics. Religious life in the household follows the mainstream Hindu, Shaiva-Vaishnava mixed calendar common in Vokkaliga farming families of the district, combining household worship of family deities with periodic visits to larger temples such as Chamundeshwari Temple on Chamundi Hills in Mysuru during Dasara, an occasion Puttaswamy treats as both devotional and a rare family outing away from the farm.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile:
Puttaswamy's most direct dealings with government run through two channels: the cooperative sugar mill and irrigation bureaucracy that decide his income, and the panchayat and revenue offices that administer welfare schemes and land records. When cane payments run late, as they have in multiple recent crushing seasons, district administrations have had to formally order sugar factories to release pending price and subsidy amounts owed to farmers, splitting a top-up payment between the state government's share and a matching contribution from the mills themselves. Puttaswamy has joined roadside protests outside mill gates organised loosely under the banner of the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha, the farmers' organisation with a strong base in Mandya, when a season's arrears stretch past what the household can absorb.

The other recurring flashpoint is water. In deficient-monsoon years, when the Cauvery Water Management Authority orders Karnataka to release water from the KRS reservoir to Tamil Nadu, farmers in Mandya have mounted sustained protests at Sanjay Circle and blocked the old Bengaluru-Mysuru highway; in one such standoff in August 2023, Karnataka initially offered to release 3,000 cusecs against a Tamil Nadu demand for 12,500 cusecs before the two sides settled on an interim release of 5,000 cusecs for fifteen days. Puttaswamy has taken part in these protests when they coincide with a season in which his own canal turn has already been cut short, experiencing the dispute as a direct threat to his second paddy crop rather than an abstract inter-state issue.

On welfare delivery, his household holds a Priority Household ration card under the state's Anna Bhagya scheme, entitling the family to a fixed quantity of free foodgrain each month on top of the earlier subsidised PDS allocation, and he has used MGNREGA job-card work on village road and canal-desilting projects in at least two lean seasons to cover a cash shortfall between crops. Land records for his holding are registered under the state's Bhoomi digitisation system, which he trusts more than he trusts the mill's payment ledger, though he has twice had to visit the taluk revenue office to correct a survey-number discrepancy affecting his share of the family's divided land. He has never contested a panchayat election himself but votes in every gram panchayat, assembly and parliamentary election, and follows Mandya's Lok Sabha and assembly results closely because, in his view, whichever party controls the state decides how fast cane arrears get paid.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile:
Puttaswamy takes evident pride in Mandya's identity as the Cauvery-irrigated sugar bowl of Karnataka, and in the legacy of the KRS dam and the Mysore-era engineer Visvesvaraya, whose modernisation projects he regards as the foundation of the irrigation system his family still depends on. At the same time, he shares a grievance documented as widespread across Mandya, Ramanagara and Chamarajanagara: a sense that the state government, however proud of Mysuru's heritage or Bengaluru's technology economy, treats agrarian distress in districts like his as secondary to the capital's priorities, a perception that persists in regional accounts even though the state's most recent chief ministers have themselves come from the region.

Asked to explain why children in villages like his sometimes leave school before finishing the tenth standard, Puttaswamy would not frame it as a failure of will on the part of families. Based on his own reasoning about Kiran's situation, he would point instead to the collision between the cane and paddy calendar and the school calendar, the cost and safety of travelling beyond the village once a child reaches PU college age, and the fact that a household already waiting on a delayed mill payment cannot easily absorb the cost of transport, books or uniforms for a second child at once; this is an inference drawn from his own household's decisions rather than a claim he has stated in exactly these words.

On water, he draws a sharp line between two disputes that outsiders sometimes conflate: the decades-old Cauvery-sharing dispute with Tamil Nadu, which he experiences directly whenever a release order cuts his canal turn, and the newer, still-unresolved Mekedatu reservoir proposal on the same river, which he supports because he understands it as a way to store more of Karnataka's own share of Cauvery water rather than release it downstream, even though he is aware Tamil Nadu and some environmental groups oppose it for different reasons. He blames the Cauvery Water Management Authority's release orders and, more diffusely, Tamil Nadu's court petitions, for the years his second paddy crop fails, while reserving a separate and more personal frustration for the sugar mills, whom he blames directly for payment delays regardless of which government is in power.

On healthcare, his frustration is less about disputes and more about distance: anything beyond a fever or minor injury means a trip to Mandya town or, for serious conditions, to Mysuru, and a day spent travelling for treatment is a day of lost farm labour the household can rarely spare. On his children's future, he wants Chaitra to finish PU college and, if possible, a diploma or degree that could lead to a government job or a position in a Bengaluru-based company, and wants Kiran to inherit the farm eventually but only after finishing secondary school, a sequencing he insists on more firmly since watching neighbours' sons abandon school permanently for cane-cutting wages. He is proud of being a farmer but does not want either of his children to depend on farming alone, a view he attributes to the unpredictability of both weather and mill payments rather than to any dissatisfaction with agrarian life itself.

name: A garment factory worker in Bengaluru Urban (Old Mysuru region)
definition: Manjula is a composite portrait of a woman working in Bengaluru's garment export industry, built from documented patterns of migration, labour and housing among the city's female industrial workforce rather than from any single real individual. She is 33 years old, born in a village in rural Mandya district, and moved to Bengaluru with her husband about fifteen years ago when construction work drew him to the city; they now rent a single room in an unauthorised residential layout near the Peenya industrial estate in Bengaluru Urban district. She belongs to a Scheduled Caste community that Census-derived lists of Karnataka's Scheduled Castes place among those present across all six Old Mysuru districts, generally in wage-labour rather than landowning households. She works as a sewing-machine operator in a garment export unit, earning close to the sector's statutory minimum wage, while her husband does daily-wage construction and auto-driving work. They have two children, a fifteen-year-old daughter in the ninth standard and a nine-year-old son, and the household's combined monthly income puts them well below Bengaluru's cost of living even as her labour underpins the export orders the city's garment sector fulfils for global apparel brands. This is an analytic composite grounded in regional labour, health and education evidence, not a record of a real person.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile:
Manjula's working day starts before 5 a.m., when she cooks the family's meals, before leaving for a garment export unit on Bengaluru's northwestern industrial fringe by around 7:30 a.m., either walking or taking a short bus ride made free under the state's Shakti scheme. Her factory is one of a large number of garment export units in and around Bengaluru that together employ a workforce estimated in the hundreds of thousands, overwhelmingly women, producing stitched garments for export brands under tight production targets set by piece-rate output per line; her nine-to-ten-hour shift is built around meeting a daily quota rather than a fixed number of tasks. Karnataka's statutory minimum wage for the garment sector stood at 10,330 rupees a month, basic plus dearness allowance, as recorded by a 2024 sector-wide labour study, and while Manjula's own wage sits close to this floor, the same study found that 61% of women workers wanted better pay, that 82% worked overtime but only 58% of those were paid fairly for it, and that 16% took on a second paid job to cover household expenses.

The toll of the work is physical as well as financial. Prolonged hours of sitting and repetitive hand movement at the sewing machine produce recurring back and shoulder pain and eye strain that she manages with over-the-counter painkillers rather than medical leave, since piece-rate systems penalise absence directly. Reporting on Karnataka's garment sector has documented a wider pattern of harsh working conditions, wages that fall well short of a living wage, and harassment, including verbal abuse from supervisors under production pressure, alongside comparatively low rates of unionisation among the mostly female workforce. Manjula is aware of unions such as the Garment Labour Union and the Karnataka Garment Workers Union that have organised in the sector, and knows co-workers who are members, but has not joined herself, partly from fear of drawing supervisor attention and partly because she cannot spare the time union meetings would require after an already long day.

On days when an export deadline is close, her shift extends into the evening, and she returns home after 8 p.m. to begin a second, unpaid shift of cooking, cleaning and helping her son with schoolwork before her daughter, who has taken over much of the housework on ordinary days, hands the household back to her. A detailed 2024 study following 184 women garment workers in Karnataka over two years found that many combine roughly nine to ten hours of factory labour with another five to six hours of domestic work daily, a combination researchers described as forcing women like Manjula to choose between time poverty and income poverty rather than escaping either.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile:
Manjula, her husband, and their two children live in a single rented room in an unauthorised layout near the Peenya industrial estate, sharing a common toilet and water connection with several neighbouring households, a housing pattern researchers describe as typical of Bengaluru's slum and informal-settlement population, where many families live in one-room dwellings of roughly 100 square feet with limited water, sanitation and drainage access. The family holds no formal tenancy document for the room, which complicates access to some address-linked government schemes and has meant at least one forced move in the past when a landlord decided to redevelop the building. Her husband's construction work is daily-wage and seasonal, drying up during the monsoon and whenever a particular site finishes, so her factory wage, though itself close to the statutory minimum, is frequently the household's only certain income in a given month; several months a year they also send a portion of earnings back to her in-laws in the native Mandya village, an obligation she and her husband consider non-negotiable regardless of their own tightness of budget.

The double burden documented among Karnataka's garment workers falls squarely on Manjula: after her factory shift she does the bulk of cooking, cleaning and childcare, work researchers have quantified at five to six additional hours a day on top of a nine-to-ten-hour shift. Increasingly, her fifteen-year-old daughter Keerthana has taken on a share of this domestic labour on days when Manjula's shift runs late, watching her younger brother, cooking the evening meal and managing chores that would otherwise fall entirely to her mother, a redistribution of labour onto a school-going daughter that is common in migrant working-class households in Bengaluru's industrial periphery but that directly competes with Keerthana's own study time. Manjula and her husband make most major decisions jointly, including about the children's schooling, but her mobility and financial autonomy are constrained by needing to be home to manage cooking and childcare around her shift timing, a constraint she describes as harder than the physical demands of factory work itself. Neither she nor her husband has extended family nearby to share caregiving; the informal support network she relies on for emergencies, such as a sick child during a work shift, is made up entirely of neighbouring women from the same layout, several of whom are also garment workers from villages elsewhere in Old Mysuru or further afield. It is this layout-based network, rather than any relative in the city, that Manjula would call on first in a genuine emergency, reflecting how thoroughly the household's day-to-day survival now depends on Bengaluru-based ties built through shared work and shared housing rather than on the kinship network that still anchors its longer-term decisions.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile:
Manjula herself studied only up to the eighth standard in her native Mandya village before her family's move to Bengaluru interrupted her schooling entirely; she was married at nineteen and never returned to formal education. Both her children are enrolled in a government Kannada-medium school within walking distance of their rented room, a choice driven by cost rather than preference, since the private English-medium schools that dominate Bengaluru's education market, and that she believes offer better job prospects, are priced well beyond the household's budget, a Kannada-versus-English tension education reporting describes as sharpened across the city by the demands of Bengaluru's private-sector job market. Her daughter Keerthana, now fifteen and in the ninth standard, is at the exact stage regional data flags as highest-risk: Karnataka's own secondary-level dropout rate for classes 9 and 10 was recorded at 22.09% in UDISE+ 2023-24 data against a 14.1% national average, and Bengaluru district has separately been identified in state education department reporting as recording among the highest absolute numbers of school dropouts in Karnataka, a distinction attributed to its large migrant and slum-dwelling child population rather than to any single cause.

For Keerthana specifically, Manjula identifies three pressures pulling against continued schooling. The first is domestic and sibling-care labour: on days when Manjula's shift runs long, Keerthana is the one who manages her younger brother, cooks, and handles household chores, time that competes directly with homework and that could, if the pattern deepens, tip toward withdrawal from school altogether. The second is safety and commuting: were Keerthana to continue past the tenth standard into a pre-university college, the nearest government college is far enough that daily travel would be necessary, and studies of migrant construction and industrial workers' children in Bengaluru have found that families' anxiety about unsupervised travel, combined with the informal, undocumented nature of many migrant households' city residence, contributes to disrupted schooling and dropout even when children were initially enrolled; migrant families that move between cities or between rural and urban addresses in search of work also frequently fail to carry a transfer certificate, which independent researchers have identified as a specific administrative barrier blocking re-enrolment in a new government school. The third, and the one Manjula worries about most directly, is economic: a garment-sector job, even at minimum wage, is an achievable and immediate income for a teenage girl in a household as financially stretched as hers, and the pull toward Keerthana eventually joining her mother's own line of work, whether at sixteen or after finishing the tenth standard, is real and openly discussed within the family, even as Manjula says she wants Keerthana to finish school first.

The state's Shakti free bus scheme is the one policy Manjula credits with concretely improving Keerthana's chances of continuing past the tenth standard: since June 2023, the scheme has let women and girls travel free on state-run buses, recording over 225 crore free rides in its first year alone and saving women passengers a combined 5,481 crore rupees in fares, and Manjula now sees a free ride to a government pre-university college, rather than a paid one, as the difference between a realistic and an unrealistic plan for her daughter's next two years of education.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile:
Manjula's own health reflects a pattern documented across Bengaluru's garment workforce: a 2025 cross-sectional study of women aged 15 to 49 employed in the city's garment factories found an overall anaemia prevalence of 71.3%, with over half of affected women moderately anaemic, a burden researchers linked to long working hours, inadequate dietary intake and poor workplace conditions rather than to any single cause. She has never been formally diagnosed, but recognises the fatigue and breathlessness the study describes, and has been advised informally by a co-worker to eat more green vegetables, advice she says she cannot always afford to follow on the household's budget. For routine illness, she and her family depend on a public primary health centre and, for anything more serious, the government general hospital, since private clinics near her layout are affordable only for a single consultation, not for sustained treatment; a household survey of a Bengaluru slum ward found that residents faced significant barriers translating even a diagnosed illness into consistent treatment, citing cost, distance, and the difficulty of taking time off daily-wage or piece-rate work.

Housing conditions compound these risks: the family's one-room rented accommodation, shared water source, and limited sanitation are typical of the overcrowded, service-poor housing researchers have documented in Bengaluru's slums and unauthorised layouts, conditions linked in local studies to elevated exposure to infectious disease and to the kind of chronic, low-grade illness that rarely becomes a medical emergency but steadily saps a household's capacity to work and save. She worries most about her son's frequent stomach upsets, which she attributes to the shared water supply, and about her own untreated joint and eye strain from years of machine stitching, which she has not sought treatment for because a day of missed factory work costs more than she believes a consultation is worth. Reproductive and maternal healthcare, including her two childbirths, were managed through the government hospital system rather than any private facility, a choice driven entirely by cost rather than preference. She has never had a workplace health check-up despite years at the same factory, and relies instead on a private pharmacist near the layout for informal advice and over-the-counter medicine whenever a family member falls ill outside the primary health centre's opening hours, a common substitute for formal consultation among women in her situation who cannot easily take unpaid time off during the working day.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile:
Manjula identifies with a Scheduled Caste community; Census-derived compilations of Karnataka's Scheduled Castes list communities present across all six Old Mysuru districts in a wage-labour relationship historically distinct from land-owning cultivating communities such as the Vokkaligas, a demographic pattern documented at the population level rather than a claim about any individual family's occupation or status today. Her sense of community operates on two, only loosely connected, registers. The first is her native village network in rural Mandya, maintained through phone calls, festival visits when the family can afford the bus fare, and the remittances she and her husband send to his parents; this network remains the source of most major life-decision support, including who her daughter might eventually marry. The second is the entirely Bengaluru-based network of women from her own and neighbouring layouts, many of them fellow garment workers who migrated from villages across Mandya, Chamarajanagara and further north, who share childcare informally, lend small sums between paydays, and accompany each other to the factory when night shifts run late.

Religiously, she is Hindu and observes festivals tied to her native village's deity as well as the wider civic calendar of her Bengaluru neighbourhood, occasionally joining in Bengaluru's Karaga festival crowds, an event regional cultural accounts describe as part of the city's cosmopolitan festival scene that contrasts with the more localised rural festival calendar of villages like the one she grew up in. She is aware of labour organisations active in Bengaluru's garment sector, including the Garment Labour Union, the Karnataka Garment Workers Union and the community-based organisation Munnade, all of which researchers documenting the sector have worked alongside to record women workers' experiences; several women in her layout are members, and she considers them a kind of informal safety net even though she has not joined herself. Caste and community shape her social ties less through formal institutions, since she has no equivalent in the city to a village-level caste association, than through the practical overlap of shared migration origin, shared workplace, and shared economic precarity among the women she lives among. She sends money home for her native village's annual temple festival even in years the family cannot attend in person, treating the contribution as a marker of continued belonging to a community she otherwise experiences mainly through memory and phone calls rather than through everyday participation in Bengaluru itself.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile:
Since September 2025, Manjula's ward on Bengaluru's northwestern industrial fringe has fallen under one of the five new city corporations that replaced the BBMP under the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, a restructuring civic-governance reporting describes as the biggest change to the city's municipal administration since BBMP's own creation, with each corporation now running its own council, mayor and commissioner under an overarching Greater Bengaluru Authority chaired by the chief minister. In practice, she has noticed little change yet in the responsiveness of local governance: garbage collection, street lighting and drainage in her unauthorised layout remain irregular, and she does not yet know which corporation's ward office to approach for a grievance, since BBMP's own council term had already lapsed years before the restructuring and ward-level elections under the new corporations are still pending.

Access to welfare schemes is complicated by the informal status of her housing. The family holds a Below Poverty Line ration card entitling them to subsidised and, under the state's Anna Bhagya scheme, additional free foodgrain each month, but registering and updating it required repeated visits to the local office because the family's rented address in an unauthorised layout is not always accepted without difficulty as proof of residence. Neither she nor her husband is formally registered for Employees' State Insurance or provident fund benefits in the way organised-sector garment employment nominally requires, a gap researchers studying Karnataka's garment workforce have documented as common, particularly among contract and informally hired workers. The Shakti scheme's free bus travel is the welfare benefit she uses most consistently, both for her own commute and for Keerthana's school and, she hopes, future college travel. Piped water does not reach her layout reliably, so the family depends on a shared borewell and occasional tanker supply arranged informally among neighbours, a pattern documented in peripheral and unauthorised parts of the city that lie outside the core municipal water utility's service area. She remains registered to vote at her native village address in Mandya rather than in Bengaluru, a common arrangement among migrant workers that means she has never voted in a BBMP or city-corporation-linked local election, only in the village's panchayat and in state and national elections when she can arrange the trip home.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile:
Manjula takes real pride in supporting her family through her own wage rather than depending entirely on her husband's irregular construction earnings, and describes her work, despite its physical toll, as something that has given her a degree of independence unavailable to women in her native village who lack access to factory employment. At the same time, she carries a documented but rarely publicly voiced frustration common among Bengaluru's garment workforce: that her labour sits at the base of an export industry serving major global apparel brands, yet her wage, close to the sector's statutory minimum, does not come close to covering the actual cost of living in the city, a gap researchers studying Karnataka's garment sector have described in terms of a wider mismatch between minimum and living wages in the industry. She blames factory management and, more distantly, the international brands that set the prices paid to the factory, for this gap, rather than the state government, whose Shakti and Anna Bhagya schemes she credits with meaningfully easing specific costs, transport and food, even if they do not address wages directly.

Asked to explain why a girl like her own daughter might leave school before finishing secondary education, Manjula would not frame it as any lack of ability or ambition on the girl's part. Based on her own household's daily pressures, she would point to the combination of sibling-care and domestic labour that falls on an older daughter when a mother works long factory shifts, the safety and cost concerns around a teenage girl commuting further for higher secondary education, and the simple, immediate availability of factory wage-work as an alternative to continued schooling in a household that cannot easily absorb years of further educational expense without an income to offset it; this is an inference drawn from her own family's circumstances rather than a view she has stated in these exact words. This framing differs in emphasis from that of a Cauvery-belt farming family, where seasonal agricultural and cane-cutting labour rather than urban commuting and domestic burden is more often the immediate pressure, a difference attributable to the sharply different economic geography of Bengaluru's migrant-industrial neighbourhoods compared with the region's agrarian taluks.

On healthcare, her frustration centres on the gap between the public hospital system she can afford, which she describes as crowded and slow, and the private facilities she cannot, a divide researchers have documented as especially stark in a city with a large concentration of private super-specialty hospitals serving a wealthier clientele alongside underfunded public facilities in poorer wards. On the city more broadly, she voices a view regional commentary describes as widespread among Bengaluru's lower-income and migrant residents: that the city's growth as a global technology and export hub has driven up her rent, her transport time, and her cost of living, without a proportionate improvement in the wages, housing security, or public services available to workers like her, whose labour, in the garment sector, is as essential to the city's export economy as software is to its technology one. She wants her daughter to finish school and, ideally, find work that does not require standing or sitting at a machine for ten hours a day, and considers this ambition realistic only if the family's finances hold steady long enough to get Keerthana through the next few years without an economic shock forcing an earlier decision.

name: A groundnut and onion farmer in Challakere taluk (Bayaluseeme region)
definition: This persona is an analytic composite of a smallholder dryland farmer in Challakere taluk, Chitradurga district, in Karnataka's Bayaluseeme (open-plains) belt within the state's Central Dry agro-climatic zone. He is about 44 years old, married, with a teenage son and a younger daughter. Communities such as the Kuruba, traditionally associated with sheep-rearing and dryland cultivation, are documented in land records and local reporting as historically dependent on the region's Amrita Mahal Kaval grazing commons, and this persona is drawn from that pattern. He farms about three rainfed acres of groundnut, onion and ragi and keeps a small flock of sheep grazed partly on the shrinking kaval commons near his village, close to land now diverted for the Challakere "science city" that hosts DRDO, ISRO, IISc and BARC facilities. His household income is small and swings sharply with the monsoon and market prices, commonly falling in the range of Rs 8,000 to Rs 14,000 a month on an annualised basis. He and his wife studied only up to middle school. This is an analytic composite built from regional evidence and documented patterns in Chitradurga district, not a real named individual; his circumstances illustrate widely reported regional conditions rather than one person's biography.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: He is a groundnut, onion and ragi farmer with about three acres of rainfed land on the dry plateau outside Challakere, the driest of Chitradurga district's six taluks [S1]. His day starts before sunrise: checking the two borewells that irrigate part of his groundnut and onion plots, moving his small flock of eight to ten sheep out to graze on whatever remains of the Amrita Mahal Kaval commons near his village, and walking his fields to check for pest damage before the heat sets in. One of his two borewells failed two years ago when the water table dropped further, a familiar story in Challakere taluk: during Karnataka's severe 2023 drought, a 22-year-old farmer in Tippareddyhalli village of the same taluk died by suicide after all four of the borewells on his land failed and he could not redeem gold he had pledged against a loan [S4]. That case sits in the background of how he and his neighbours talk about debt and water. His own approach has been to diversify rather than double down: groundnut and onion in rotation with ragi, plus sheep as a buffer that can be sold in a bad crop year, because prices for both his main cash crops are volatile. In drought years, farmers across Chitradurga and Challakere are forced down to a single crop a season; when an unusually good monsoon later brings a bumper second crop, the resulting oversupply has crashed retail onion prices from as high as Rs 40-50 a kilogram to as low as Rs 5-10 a kilogram within weeks, wiping out the margin many farmers, including him, had counted on [S5]. Groundnut prices are similarly unstable, with recent mandi price data for Karnataka showing quintal rates ranging from under Rs 4,000 to over Rs 7,000 depending on the season and quality grade [S7]. Around 10,000 acres of the taluk's kaval grazing commons were diverted between 2009 and 2010 for a government "science city" hosting DRDO, ISRO, BARC and IISc facilities, shrinking the open land he and other herding families once used freely for sheep and cattle [S2][S3]. He now negotiates informally with neighbours for grazing access and sometimes walks his flock further than before. During the fallow months and drought years, he and his wife register for work under MGNREGA, the rural employment guarantee scheme, though a 2025 assessment of the programme in Karnataka found that a shrinking central budget allocation had cut the average days of work available per registered household to roughly half of the 100 days nominally promised, so the scheme supplements rather than replaces farm income [S6]. Across a full year, his household's income is small and uneven, commonly falling somewhere between Rs 8,000 and Rs 14,000 a month once averaged over good and bad seasons, before loan repayments.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: He is married, in his mid-forties, with two children: a son of about sixteen studying in a government high school in Challakere town, and a daughter of about thirteen in a nearby government school. His wife works alongside him on the farm and manages the sheep, in addition to unpaid domestic labour and childcare, a division of labour that mirrors the pattern documented across Chitradurga district, where the 2011 Census recorded a female literacy rate of about 65.9% against a male literacy rate of about 81.4%, a gap that reflects historic disparities in schooling access rather than any inherent difference between men and women [S1]. He and his wife both studied only up to middle school before leaving to help on family land. His household is part of a wider kin network of Kuruba families in and around his village who, in accounts gathered by reporters and researchers, describe having depended for generations on the Amrita Mahal Kaval commons to graze cattle and sheep alongside dryland cultivation [S2]. Roughly 500 farming and pastoral families across some 70 villages in Challakere taluk are documented as having lost grazing access when kaval land was diverted for the science city project beginning in 2009-2010, and many of these families, including his own extended relatives, describe a shift toward smaller flocks and more wage labour as a result [S2]. His parents live nearby and help with childcare and light farm tasks; his elderly father was among the villagers who joined protests against the land acquisition when it began [S3]. Decisions in the household are made jointly with his wife on day-to-day matters, though he manages loan and land transactions, a pattern researchers and reporters describe as typical of smallholder dryland households in this belt, where women's labour is central to production but formal land ownership and credit access remain concentrated with men. He hopes his son will finish school and either continue farming with additional land he plans to lease, or find work outside agriculture; he is less certain about his daughter's path beyond secondary school, given the household's tight finances and the distance to the nearest junior college in Challakere or Chitradurga town. Marriage in the household followed the common local pattern of a match arranged between families within the same community, and he expects, without having fixed a date, that his daughter's marriage will similarly be arranged sometime after she completes schooling, though he says the family is in no hurry given how much her labour and her brother's continued schooling both depend on the household's finances holding steady over the next few years. Festivals and life-cycle events such as naming ceremonies, weddings and harvest observances remain the occasions when his wider extended family, many of them also dryland farmers and small herders in nearby villages, gather together, and these gatherings are also where informal advice on borewell contractors, land leases and children's schooling options circulates fastest.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: He completed schooling up to Class 7 before leaving to work on the family farm when his own father's health declined; his wife studied to about the same level. Their son, about sixteen, is currently enrolled in a government high school in Challakere town, commuting daily by bicycle or shared transport over several kilometres of rural road since there is no functioning secondary school within walking distance of their hamlet. Their daughter, thirteen, is in a government upper-primary school closer to home, but the family already discusses what will happen when she reaches Class 9 and must transfer to the same distant high school her brother attends, since no secondary school for girls exists nearer their village. This kind of distance-driven risk is a well-documented driver of dropout in Karnataka: UDISE+ data for 2023-24 put the state's overall dropout rate at classes 9-10 at 22.2%, far above the national average and among the worst in south India, a gap officials and researchers link partly to the distance between villages and the nearest functioning secondary school [S1][S2]. Girls have faced a somewhat sharper version of this risk in recent years: the same UDISE+ series recorded a secondary-level dropout rate among girls in Karnataka of 19.6% in 2023-24, improving to 13.9% by 2025-26 but still tied with Assam for the highest rate among India's larger states, well above states like Kerala (about 3%) and Tamil Nadu (about 3.2%) [S3]. In villages like his, the reasons that surface locally echo ones documented for the wider Bayaluseeme belt: the cost and distance of transport to a taluk-headquarters school, the pull of farm and grazing labour during the groundnut harvest and lambing season, and, in his own community's specific case, the disruption caused by the 2009-2010 diversion of Amrita Mahal Kaval grazing land for the Challakere science city, which researchers and reporters have noted altered pastoralist families' daily routines in ways that can pull children, particularly boys who help move livestock, away from regular schooling [S4]. In bad drought years, when farm income collapses, families across this dry-zone belt, including his own on occasion, sometimes draw a teenage child into short stretches of paid daily-wage work without formally withdrawing them from the school rolls, a slow-attrition pattern consistent with the wider dropout figures cited above rather than a single dramatic withdrawal [S1][S2]. He has not had to place his daughter in a residential school, but he is aware of the Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV) scheme, which the central government runs to provide residential secondary schooling for girls from disadvantaged households in educationally backward blocks, and he sees it as a fallback if the family cannot manage her daily commute once she reaches high school [S5]. He wants both children to finish Class 10, and ideally his son to complete a diploma or ITI course rather than depend solely on farming, given how unpredictable groundnut and onion income has become; for his daughter, his ambitions are more guarded, shaped by the practical worry that a distant high school, exam-season expenses, and the ongoing need for her labour at home during peak agricultural periods could combine to end her schooling earlier than his son's.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: His health concerns are mostly occupational and financial rather than acute. Years of fieldwork under direct sun, without much protective equipment, expose him to heat stress during the hottest months before the monsoon, and he applies pesticides on his groundnut crop with minimal protective gear, a pattern documented broadly among Indian farmers: reporting on climate change's effect on Indian agriculture has noted that hotter, more erratic growing seasons are pushing farmers toward heavier pesticide use even as protective equipment remains unaffordable or impractical to wear in the heat [S1]. He has had bouts of skin irritation and headaches after spraying, which he attributes to the chemicals, though he has not sought a formal diagnosis. For routine illness, his family relies on a primary health centre a few kilometres away, part of Chitradurga district's network of PHCs, community health centres and the district hospital in Chitradurga town, which the district administration describes as offering free consultations, basic tests and immunisation [S2]; anything serious means travelling further, generally to Chitradurga town or to the Basaveshwara Medical College and Hospital, run under the trust of the Murugha Mutt, the Veerashaiva-Lingayat institution headed for decades by seer Shivamurthy Murugha Sharanaru, which functions as the district's main teaching hospital [S3]. The financial stress of farming under drought and debt weighs on him, and he is aware, through village conversation and local news, of the wider pattern of farmer suicides that swept Karnataka's dry-zone districts during the severe 2023 drought, including a widely discussed case from Tippareddyhalli village in his own taluk, where a young farmer took his life after his borewells failed and he could not redeem pledged gold; state compensation data show that of 1,182 farmer suicides recorded statewide between April 2023 and July 2024, most were linked to drought, crop failure and debt [S4]. He describes this less as a personal risk he expects to face and more as a shared, low hum of anxiety that shapes how cautiously he borrows and how much he worries in a bad year. His wife, who does the bulk of the physically repetitive work of weeding, sheep-tending and unpaid domestic labour on top of fieldwork, has chronic back and joint pain that she manages without regular medical attention, treating it as an ordinary cost of her work rather than a condition worth a clinic visit.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: He identifies with the Kuruba community, one of the groups that land records, local reporting and researchers describe as having traditionally depended on the Amrita Mahal Kaval grazing commons around Challakere for pastoral livelihoods alongside dryland farming, a characterisation attributed to these sources rather than treated as an inherent trait of the community [S1]. His sense of collective identity is shaped as much by this shared relationship to the kaval land and its erosion as by caste alone: he is part of a loose network of herding and farming families across dozens of villages in Challakere taluk who have watched roughly 10,000 acres of common grazing land diverted since 2009-2010 for the government's "science city" hosting DRDO, ISRO, BARC and IISc facilities, and who describe a shared, still-unresolved grievance about the loss of grazing access and the compensation and consultation they say they were not adequately given [S1][S2]. He is Hindu, and Veerashaiva-Lingayat institutions loom large in the district's religious and civic landscape even though he is not part of that community himself: the Murugha Mutt in Chitradurga town, headed for decades by seer Shivamurthy Murugha Sharanaru, runs well over a hundred schools, hostels and colleges, including the medical college that serves as the district's main referral hospital, and he has relatives who have studied or received free hostel accommodation through mutt-run institutions even though his own children have not [S3]. Locally, he attends festivals at the village's own deity temple and occasionally travels to larger regional fairs; caste associations and village elders' councils remain the main forums where disputes over land, grazing rights and marriage are informally settled, alongside the more distant and formal channels of the taluk administration. He describes the region's politics of reservation and community identity, including debates over Vokkaliga, Lingayat and internal Scheduled Tribe classification, as something he follows through conversation and local news rather than active involvement, since his more immediate daily preoccupation remains land, water and the price his crops fetch at the market rather than caste politics as such. Civic activity formed around the kaval dispute itself, including the protests villagers mounted against the original land transfer, has given his community a further, more issue-specific form of collective belonging alongside caste and religion, one built around a shared grievance over land rather than a shared institution [S1][S2]. He does not describe himself as devout in a formal sense, observing festivals and temple visits more as markers of the agricultural and social calendar than as a matter of close religious practice, and he is careful, when the subject comes up, to describe the science-city land dispute and grazing-rights debates in terms of his own family's documented losses rather than blanket claims about any single community's character.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: His main interactions with the state are through agricultural input subsidies, drought and crop-loss compensation claims, and MGNREGA job-card registration, all channelled through the village panchayat and the taluk office in Challakere. He has filed for drought-relief compensation in past bad years and describes the process as slow and paperwork-heavy, consistent with wider reporting on Karnataka's compensation systems, where state data show that of 1,182 farmer suicides recorded between April 2023 and July 2024, only 1,003 were deemed eligible for the promised Rs 5 lakh compensation and disbursement to eligible families lagged behind approvals [S1]. His household has repeatedly registered for MGNREGA work during the lean season, though he and his wife have found that the number of days of paid work actually available has shrunk over recent years, consistent with a 2025 Karnataka-wide assessment showing the average number of workdays per household falling as the central government's budget allocation for the scheme declined by nearly half over six years [S2]. He remains closely engaged with the long-running dispute over the Amrita Mahal Kaval land diverted for the Challakere science city: he recalls villagers protesting the original 2009-2010 land transfer and follows any news about past environmental and regulatory interventions in the project, since further diversion of the remaining kaval land would directly affect his own grazing access [S3][S4]. His wife and daughter benefit from the state's Shakti scheme, which gives women free travel on government buses; his wife occasionally uses it to travel to the taluk headquarters for panchayat or bank business, part of a scheme that state data show had delivered well over two hundred crore free rides to women within its first year [S5]. He votes in state and panchayat elections and is aware, in general terms, of the long-standing classification of parts of this belt, including Kolar, as comparatively "backward" under the 2002 Nanjundappa Committee's district and taluk rankings, though he is uncertain whether that older classification has been updated or whether it still shapes where new investment goes [S6]. He deals with the local panchayat mainly for land-record queries, drought-relief applications and disputes over grazing access, and he attends gram sabha meetings when farming permits, mainly to raise concerns about the kaval land dispute, borewell electricity connections and the condition of the road linking his hamlet to Challakere town, treating these practical, recurring items as the real measure of local government's performance in his village rather than broader ideological debates.

On healthcare, he would likely frame the problem as one of distance rather than absence: a primary health centre exists nearby, but anything serious means a trip to Chitradurga town, an inconvenient and costly journey for a farmer without reliable transport. He would probably demand more consistent drought and crop-loss compensation, faster disbursal of relief payments, and continued or restored access to the kaval grazing land for herding families like his own, seeing this as a specific, addressable grievance rather than a vague complaint. He describes himself, in the account this composite draws on, as neither anti-development nor uncritically supportive of projects like the science city, but as someone whose family's stake in the outcome — displaced grazing land against uncertain local jobs — has not yet been resolved to his satisfaction, a widely shared rather than fringe sentiment among Challakere's pastoral and farming families according to available reporting [S2][S3].

name: A sericulture worker in Chintamani taluk (Bayaluseeme region)
definition: This persona is an analytic composite of a woman engaged in mulberry-based sericulture and seasonal agricultural wage labour in Chintamani taluk, Chikkaballapur district, part of the Kolar-Chikkaballapur Telugu borderland within Karnataka's Bayaluseeme belt. She is about 34 years old, married, with a son of about fifteen and a daughter of about fourteen. Chintamani taluk borders Andhra Pradesh and is documented as a Telugu-Kannada bilingual area with one of the district's larger areas under mulberry cultivation, part of a district-wide sericulture sector supporting over 15,000 farming families. She and her family are landless or near-landless agricultural labourers who rear silkworms on a small, rented mulberry patch and take daily wage work in tomato, grape and other vegetable fields during the agricultural season. Her husband migrates seasonally to brick kilns and construction sites, a pattern documented among families in Chikkaballapur and Kolar's border taluks. This is an analytic composite grounded in regional evidence and documented patterns in Chikkaballapur district's sericulture and border-taluk economy, not a real named individual; her circumstances illustrate widely reported conditions in this specific sub-region rather than one person's biography.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Her day is split between two forms of labour that rarely let up: tending the family's rented quarter-acre of mulberry and rearing silkworms at home, and taking daily wage work in the fields of larger landholders growing tomato, grape or vegetables nearer Chintamani town. Chintamani taluk, which borders Andhra Pradesh, is one of Chikkaballapur district's key centres for sericulture; the district as a whole has roughly 13,360 hectares under mulberry cultivation spread across some 1,131 villages, supporting more than 15,000 farming families [S1][S2]. Her mornings begin before sunrise: she cuts and carries mulberry leaves to feed the silkworms several times a day during the roughly month-long rearing cycle, cleans the rearing trays and manages the temperature and humidity of the shed by hand, tasks that studies of the sericulture workforce describe as falling disproportionately on women, who dominate cocoon harvesting, worm-mounting, leaf-feeding and rearing operations even though men usually handle marketing the cocoons at the local market [S3]. When there is no active rearing batch, she takes daily wage work transplanting or harvesting in nearby tomato and grape fields, work that is physically demanding and paid by the day, with no guarantee of work on a given morning. Her husband combines farm labour with seasonal migration: during the agricultural off-season he travels to brick kilns or construction sites, sometimes locally and sometimes further away, a pattern of seasonal brick-kiln and construction migration widely documented among landless families in this border belt, though the most detailed published research on its educational and economic impact comes from brick-kiln workforces in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh rather than Karnataka-specific surveys [S4]. Their combined household income is small and irregular, typically in the range of Rs 6,000-10,000 a month when averaged across active rearing cycles, wage-labour days and her husband's migration earnings, with gaps during the lean months between cocoon crops. The couple's earnings depend heavily on the cocoon market price at the Chintamani grainage (seed-cocoon) market, which fluctuates with silk demand and the quality grade of the cocoons produced, so a poor rearing cycle, disease among the silkworms, or a market dip can wipe out weeks of unpaid labour investment. She also manages the household's domestic work, cooking, water collection and childcare on top of both forms of paid labour, a double burden that studies of women's role in the sericulture sector describe as a defining constraint on women's ability to earn, rest or access training [S3].

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: She is 34, married for about seventeen years, with a son of fifteen studying in a government high school and a daughter of fourteen who recently completed Class 8. Her household is landless or near-landless, renting a small mulberry patch rather than owning cultivable land, a pattern common among agricultural-labour families in this belt. She and her husband are part of Chintamani taluk's Telugu-Kannada bilingual population; the taluk borders Andhra Pradesh and both Telugu and Kannada are spoken locally alongside Urdu in the town [S1]. Chikkaballapur district recorded a sex ratio of about 972 women per 1,000 men and an overall literacy rate of about 70% in the 2011 Census, with a documented gender gap in schooling completion that shapes her own biography: she studied only to about Class 6 before being needed at home to help her mother with younger siblings and domestic work, a common trajectory for girls in landless agricultural households in the district [S2]. Her husband's seasonal absence for brick-kiln or construction work means she runs the household largely alone for weeks or months at a time, managing the mulberry plot, any active silkworm-rearing cycle, wage-labour commitments and the children's schooling. Her mother-in-law, who lives with them, helps with childcare and light domestic tasks but is now elderly and limited in what she can do. Decisions about the children's schooling, health spending and daily household budgeting fall mostly to her during her husband's absences, though larger decisions such as taking a loan or moving are made jointly when he is home. She has occasionally taken her daughter along to help with mulberry-leaf cutting and silkworm feeding during particularly labour-intensive rearing cycles, especially when her husband is away and wage-labour commitments compete for her own time, a dual demand on her labour and her daughter's that studies of women's role in South Indian sericulture describe as a structural feature of the industry, noting that sericulture work is considered well suited to unskilled family labour, including women and children, precisely because it can be organised around the household [S3]. She hopes her son will complete Class 10 and find work outside agriculture and sericulture, given how unpredictable both wage labour and cocoon prices are; she wants the same for her daughter but is far less certain it will happen.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: She reached about Class 6 before leaving school to help at home, and her husband completed middle school. Their son is currently in a government high school in Chintamani town, commuting daily; their daughter finished Class 8 at the local government upper-primary school, and the family is now weighing whether she will continue into Class 9, the point at which Karnataka's dropout data turn sharply worse. UDISE+ figures put the state's overall dropout rate in classes 9-10 at 22.2% for 2023-24, well above the national average, and the dropout rate specifically among girls in Karnataka at 19.6% that year, falling to 13.9% by 2025-26 but still tied with Assam for the highest rate among India's major states, well above Kerala's roughly 3% and Tamil Nadu's roughly 3.2% [S1][S2][S3]. Several of the pressures documented for this specific part of the region converge in her daughter's case. First, distance and safety: the nearest high school offering Classes 9 and 10 is several kilometres from their hamlet, on a route that runs through or near the town centre, and parents in border taluks like Chintamani weigh the daily commute and the perceived safety of adolescent daughters heavily when deciding whether to continue their education past Class 8. Second, labour: the household's sericulture cycle requires intensive, time-bound leaf-feeding and rearing labour that studies of the industry describe as disproportionately performed by women and, often, by daughters pulled in during particularly demanding rearing batches, especially in households like hers where the father migrates seasonally for brick-kiln or construction work and is unavailable to share the load [S4]. A 2003 Human Rights Watch investigation into India's silk industry, though dated, documented an industry-wide risk of children being drawn into cocoon and silk-related labour in ways that displace schooling, a historical pattern that continues to shape local expectations of what a teenage daughter's time should go toward during the sericulture season, even where formal bonded child labour is not present [S5]. Third, seasonal migration: her husband's brick-kiln and construction migration is part of a broader pattern of seasonal labour migration documented among landless families in India's brick-kiln workforce — the most detailed published research on this comes from neighbouring Andhra Pradesh rather than Karnataka specifically — showing that children in migrant-labour households face irregular attendance and are often pulled between their native village's school and the migration destination, weakening their attachment to a single school and raising dropout risk even when the family does not travel together every season [S6]. She is aware of the Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya scheme, the central government's residential school programme for adolescent girls from disadvantaged households in educationally backward blocks, and sees it, if a place is available, as one of the few realistic ways her daughter could continue into Class 9 and 10 without a risky daily commute or a further drain on her own labour at home during the sericulture season [S7]. She wants her daughter to finish secondary school, but describes the decision as genuinely undecided, dependent on whether a KGBV or similar hostel seat becomes available, how the next few cocoon cycles pay, and whether her husband's migration income holds up.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Her most immediate documented health risk is fluoride exposure through groundwater. Chikkaballapur district, including Chikkaballapur taluk itself, has been the subject of published water-quality studies finding that fluoride concentrations in a large share of tested groundwater and borewell samples exceed safe drinking-water limits; a 2024 study found that roughly 40% of tested groundwater samples in Chikkaballapur taluk exceeded acceptable fluoride limits, a contamination level associated with a documented risk of dental and skeletal fluorosis [S1], and a separate geochemical study of groundwater across Kolar and Tumkur districts found similarly fluoride-enriched aquifers linked to the region's granite geology [S2]. Her own taluk, Chintamani, sits on comparable dry-zone granite terrain, though she is not aware of a published survey as detailed as the one for Chikkaballapur taluk itself, so she describes her family's concern about tap and borewell water as based on shared local experience — mottled teeth among some children in her village — rather than a study she has seen herself. Occupationally, her sericulture work exposes her to repetitive strain: cutting and carrying mulberry leaves, standing for long hours over rearing trays, and handling cocoons, tasks that studies of women in South Indian sericulture link to musculoskeletal disorders, back and joint pain, skin irritation and eye strain among rearers [S3]. Her husband's periodic pesticide use on wage-labour farm assignments is a further household health concern; a study specifically examining pesticide-exposed farmers in Chikkaballapur district documented common complaints including headaches, skin irritation and respiratory symptoms following application, with protective equipment rarely used because of cost and discomfort in the heat [S4]. For routine healthcare, the family relies on a local primary health centre; the nearest major referral hospital for anything serious is R.L. Jalappa Hospital in Tamaka, Kolar, which explicitly serves as the primary tertiary referral centre for Kolar district and the bordering areas of Chikkaballapur, a journey of an hour or more from Chintamani [S5]. She manages her own chronic back pain from years of rearing-tray work largely without medical attention, treating it as an unavoidable part of the job rather than something worth the cost and travel time of a clinic visit.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: She lives in a Telugu-Kannada bilingual community typical of Chintamani taluk, which borders Andhra Pradesh; Kannada, Telugu and, in the town's older core, Urdu are all spoken locally, a linguistic mix documented for this specific taluk that distinguishes it from the Kannada-only interior of the district [S1]. She and her family are Hindu, and her sense of community is anchored less in a single caste institution than in the shared, everyday networks of sericulture: women in her hamlet who rear silkworms together, share mulberry cuttings, and informally advise each other on managing disease outbreaks among the worms, alongside kinship and neighbourhood ties. This mirrors a broader documented pattern in which sericulture functions as a female-centred rural occupation that structures women's social ties as much as their labour [S2]. She attends the local village temple's annual festival and smaller household pujas, and relies on informal women's networks, rather than a mutt or formal religious institution, as her main source of social support and information — a contrast with the more mutt-centred civic life documented further south and west in the Bayaluseeme belt around Tumakuru and Chitradurga. Politically and socially, Chintamani constituency has, in recent reporting, been described as marked by visible anti-incumbency sentiment and local frustration over unfulfilled development promises, a mood she shares in a general sense even though she does not describe herself as politically active [S3]. She sees her identity as shaped as much by her occupation and border-taluk bilingual upbringing as by caste or religion narrowly defined, and she is wary of generalisations, having heard outsiders assume, incorrectly, that everyone in her district speaks only Kannada, or that sericulture work is easy, low-effort "cottage" labour rather than the physically demanding, day-and-night rearing-cycle work it actually is. Her closest social ties are with a handful of neighbouring women who rear silkworms on a similar small scale, with whom she coordinates leaf-cutting schedules, shares child-minding when a rearing cycle demands constant attention, and exchanges practical knowledge that rarely reaches her from any formal extension service. Weddings and other life-cycle events in her family are still arranged between known families within the same broad community, a pattern typical of landless agricultural-labour households in the border taluks, and these occasions, along with the village temple's annual festival, are the main settings in which her wider kin network gathers and in which informal information about schooling options, migration contacts and hostel seats for daughters circulates.
